preamble: Loss of glottalization in the glottalized labio-velar approximant [wˀ] (Americanist w̓). It is part of a wider loss of glottalized resonants on the Northwest Coast. In Makah the Proto-Southern-Wakashan glottalized sonorants merged with the plain ones, with compensatory lengthening of the preceding vowel (Davidson 2002: 76, citing Jacobsen 1968): Nuu-chah-nulth cuw̓it, Makah cu·wit 'silver salmon'. Upriver Halkomelem lost resonant glottalization, usually lengthening the preceding vowel, while Island and Downriver keep it (Compton & Gerdts c. 2005). No Upriver word is listed for w̓: in the lexical suffix 'house', Pincott (2021: 50) gives Chilliwack =ɛ́:w̓ txʷ, =ɛ́w̓ txʷ, =əwtxʷ, which mostly keep w̓, and reconstructs Proto-Central Salish *=aw=txʷ with plain w. For the Chimakuan languages, the correspondence table in Wikipedia's Chimakuan languages article (after Powell 1974) gives the reflexes of the glottalized resonants as R or ʔR, *w̓ appearing in Quileute as w or ʔw. The Quileute words in the same article's numeral table, such as ƚáʔw 'two', show a glottal stop followed by a plain w, so the glottalization may survive as a separate segment rather than be lost; they are not listed as examples here. According to the same table, Chemakum instead hardened *w̓ to (ʔ)kʷ.

languageExamples.context: Davidson (2002: 76): the Proto-Southern-Wakashan glottalized sonorants merged with the plain sonorants in Makah, with compensatory lengthening of the preceding vowel (citing Jacobsen 1968); Nuu-chah-nulth keeps them. Werle (2010: 4) lists the "loss of glottalized resonants in Makah with concomitant lengthening of a preceding vowel"

examples.note: Davidson (2002: 76), ex. (127). The long u· before w is the compensatory lengthening.

Werle (2010: 17), ex. (71). Ditidaht duw̓aqs keeps the glottalization. The long uˑ before w matches the lengthening that Werle (2010: 4) gives as the Makah reflex of the glottalized resonants. The Wiktionary appendix of Fortescue's (2007) reconstructions has Proto-Wakashan *ʔu(ː)w̍(i)-/ʔaw̍(i)- 'father', a root without the initial n̓- or d-.
